name: Gododdin
anchor: between Din Eidyn (Edinburgh) and Traprain Law
first_written: The name comes from the Votadini of Roman-period Greek texts; the kingdom is known from the poem Y Gododdin, set around 600 and surviving in a manuscript of the later 13th century.

name: Alt Clut (later Strathclyde)
first_written: Saint Patrick's letter to Ceretic, king of Alt Clut, in the late 5th century.

name: Rheged
anchor: the Solway, between Galloway and Carlisle (both proposed)
first_written: Poems attributed to Taliesin call Urien "Ruler of Rheged" in the later 6th century; its borders are not described in any source.
checked_phrase: its borders are not described in any of them

name: Elmet
anchor: Wikipedia article coordinates (Sherburn in Elmet area)
first_written: Bede's silva Elmete and the Historia Brittonum, which says Edwin expelled its king Certic (early 7th century).

name: Ebrauc
first_written: Doubtful as a kingdom: inferred from York's Roman name and later Welsh tradition.

name: Gwynedd
first_written: The 5th-century Cantiorix inscription at Penmachno seems to be the earliest record of the name; Gildas attacks its king Maglocunus (Maelgwn).

name: Powys
first_written: Its earliest rulers are known mainly from much later sources such as the Harleian genealogies.
checked_phrase: known primarily from much later sources

name: Pengwern
first_written: Named in later Welsh poetry about Cynddylan (6th and 7th centuries); its exact location is unknown.

name: Dyfed
first_written: Gildas attacks its king Vortipor; a stone at Castell Dwyran of about 550, in Latin and ogham, may name the same king. Its royal line was founded by Irish settlers.
checked_phrase: founded by Irish settlers in the 5th century

name: Brycheiniog
first_written: Founded in legend by Brychan in the mid 5th century; probably founded by Irish raiders in the late 5th century.

name: Ergyng
anchor: Archenfield, near the Roman town of Ariconium
first_written: Named after the Roman town of Ariconium; later called Archenfield by the English.

name: Glywysing
first_written: Named in medieval Welsh tradition after an early king Glywys; descended from the Silures.

name: Gwent
first_written: The Silures article says their territory later developed into the 5th-century kingdoms of Gwent, Brycheiniog and Gwynllŵg.

name: Dumnonia
first_written: Gildas (6th century) calls it Damnonia and attacks its ruler Constantine.
checked_phrase: used by Gildas in the 6th century

name: Dál Riata
first_written: Said to be founded by the legendary Fergus Mór in the 5th century; Dunadd is thought to be its capital.
checked_phrase: founded by the legendary king Fergus

name: Picts (Fortriu)
first_written: The Verturiones were first documented by Ammianus Marcellinus in the late 4th century.
checked_phrase: first documented in the late 4th century

name: Bernicia
first_written: The first Anglian king in the record is Ida, said to have taken the kingdom about 547.

name: Deira
first_written: Bede wrote of Deira in his Ecclesiastical History, completed in 731.

name: Lindsey
first_written: Bede says Paulinus was received by the praefectus of Lindum in 625.

name: East Angles
first_written: The first reference is in the Whitby Life of St Gregory, about 704 to 713.

name: Essex
first_written: Bede notes Bishop Mellitus arriving in London in 604; a king list gives Æscwine from 527.

name: Kent
first_written: The earliest recorded king is Æthelberht, late 6th century; Augustine arrived in 597.
checked_phrase: earliest recorded king of Kent was Æthelberht

name: Sussex
first_written: The foundation legend in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle has Ælle landing in 477; historians are divided over whether he existed.
checked_phrase: Historians are divided over whether or not Ælle really existed

name: Gewisse (later Wessex)
first_written: The name is first documented in the 8th century; their first location was the upper Thames around Dorchester.
checked_phrase: first documented as Gewissorum in the eighth century
